title: 6 款开源 LLM 通过了污染检测，但这并不意味着它们没有受到污染
author: Utkarsh Mangal

Shuffle the Questions to Catch an LLM That Memorized Its Benchmark

Two short Python functions and a free Colab GPU score a model in about half an hour; a z above 3 merits a look, while a near-zero score is more of a shrug.

Utkarsh Mangal
November 26, 20269 min read
Prefer us on Google

A new model drops and initially performs well on a benchmark. Someone then asks whether it has simply "cheated" by having already seen the benchmark.

Whilst labs claim that they remove text from the benchmark from their training data, we cannot independently confirm this as access to training data is restricted. All we have are a model’s weights and a benchmark. Surprisingly, these are enough to learn something.

Basically, text is ordered. If a model has learnt a benchmark verbatim then it is likely to have also learnt its order. And this is what we can search for. Oren et al. proposed such a method [1]. To further my own understanding, I reproduced this finding.

I deliberately contaminated a small model so that I knew the correct answer. I then tested this on six open models. The first of these performed better than I had hoped. However, the second showed me how to cheat at testing. I continue to ponder the implications of this result.

Why order is important

For the 1319 primary school mathematics problems that comprise the GSM8K test set [2], the order is always the same. Take four consecutive problems from this. These four can be permuted in 24 different ways.

If a model has had no previous exposure to a benchmark then it should have no preference for any permutation. As the four problems have no connection, all permutations are equally valid and so the original order is just one of these.

However, if a model has learnt a benchmark verbatim then it will recognise the original order as more natural. Imagine being given a seemingly randomly shuffled pack of cards. Yet when you spread them out you realise they are in manufacturer order. Clearly, you would no longer trust the shuffle.

From order to a p-value

Divide a benchmark into sequential ‘shards’. For each shard, generate 10 random permutations. Alongside these, include the original order. For each of these, calculate the precise log probability that the model assigns to the whole text. As all permutations contain the same tokens, they are all the same length. Only the order differs.

Next, determine how many of the 10 permutations are outperformed by the original order. Let us call this quantity q. For a model with no prior benchmark exposure, q is uniformly distributed between 0 and 10. Therefore, we know its mean and variance. Summing together q values for n shards allows us to convert this into a z score:

z= ∑i=1n qi−nR/2 nR(R+2)/12 z = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} q_i - nR/2}{\sqrt{nR(R+2)/12}}

Where R is the number of permutations generated per shard (10 in my tests). A large positive z score indicates that, more frequently than would be expected by chance alone, the original order outperforms other orders.

Rather than accept statistics at face value, I carried out 4000 simulations of pure noise. For each, I created 40 shards and 10 permutations. Overall, 5.1% and 1.05% of these were identified as significant (p<0.05 and p<0.01 respectively). This is as expected from a fair test. Altogether, this can be expressed in a few lines:

python 
import numpy as np, torchfrom scipy import stats@torch.no_grad()def order_logprobs(model, seqs):    x = torch.tensor(seqs, device="cuda")    logits = model(x).logits[:, :-1].float()    lp = torch.log_softmax(logits, -1).gather(-1, x[:, 1:, None]).squeeze(-1)    return lp.sum(1).cpu().numpy()  def contamination_z(lp_original, lp_shuffled):    n, R = lp_shuffled.shape    q = (lp_shuffled < lp_original[:, None]).sum(1)       z = (q.sum() - n * R / 2) / np.sqrt(n * R * (R + 2) / 12)    return z, stats.norm.sf(z)

There is one distinction from the paper. Whereas Oren et al. compare the original order to the mean of permutations and carry out a t-test on shards [1], I opted for a ranked variant of this as it has an exact null distribution. I calculated both of these statistics.

Contaminating a model on purpose

Without the ability to identify something, a test’s ability to show that nothing has been identified is limited. Thus, prior to my experimentation with actual models, I set up a scenario where I knew the correct answer.

Pythia-410M was trained on the Pile — a dataset from 2020 [3][4]. GSM8K was introduced in 2021 and so this model could not have been exposed to it. I then separated 48 GSM8K test shards. Of these, 24 were sequentially trained on and the remaining 24 were reserved. Following this, I tested both sets of shards at 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 epochs of training.

Prior to training, the reserve and training shards both had a z score of -0.8. Nothing was identified. After one epoch of training, however, the z score was 5.7 (p<10⁻⁸). For 58% of shards, the original order outperformed all 10 permutations — compared to the ~9% expected by chance. Furthermore, by epochs epochs the original order was superior in all 24 shards. The text loss had fallen to 0.14 nats/token from 2.08.

As for the reserve shards, their z scores ranged between -1.8 and 1.5 across the five training points. Crucially, none of these crossed the p=0.05 significance level despite the model’s steadily deteriorating performance on this text (text loss increased to 2.69 from 2.05). Thus, the test successfully highlighted areas of exposure and ignored areas of non-exposure.

Outsmarting my test

I trained another model branch using the same 24 shards for the same number of epochs. However, within each shard, I altered the order of questions each epoch. Despite this, the model continued to correctly answer all questions and provide all answers. Crucially, the order of these was never repeated.

Refer again to Figure 2’s right-hand side. The loss for the reordered model branch is very similar to that for the original order branch (0.13 vs 0.14 nats/token at eight epochs). Both perform equally well on this text. Now consider the left hand side. At eight epochs, the reordered model branch has a z score of 0.1.

Interestingly, at four epochs the reordered model branch had a z score of 2.0 (p~0.02). However, I would not place great weight on this. With 3 lines, 5 training points, and 24 shards, occasionally an anomalous peak such as this will occur. Significantly, at the same training point the reserve shards — which the model had never been trained on — reached a z score of 1.5.

This is therefore not a statistical failure. Testing presumes that, for a model with no prior benchmark exposure, all permutations are equally probable. This can only be invalidated by something that is order sensitive. Had a model learnt all questions in a benchmark but failed to learn their order, then the test would have nothing on which to base its findings. Likewise, if a benchmark had seeped into a model’s training in an unsequenced manner (such as in disjoint web pages, forum threads and reordered versions), this would appear indistinguishable from my reordered model branch.

Therefore, a significant result is highly indicative. Conversely, a non-significant result is more akin to a shrug.

Six real models

Finally, I tested six models (Pythia-1.4B, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, TinyLlama-1.1B, SmolLM2-1.7B and Phi-2) on both GSM8K and ARC-Challenge [5]. Again, these were tested in original order. Each test involved 40 shards and 10 permutations. Altogether, this represents 160 GSM8K and 240 ARC questions — from a total of 1319 and 1172 respectively. All models were run in fp16. As previously explained, Pythia acts as the ‘clean’ model for GSM8K.

Alongside this, all models were also tested on a once-permuted, seed-fixed version of GSM8K. This permutation does not appear in any file. Were a model to respond to it then my testing process would be fabricating results.

No significant results were obtained. The highest z score was 2.0 (p=0.023) for SmolLM2-1.7B on ARC-Challenge. Interestingly, this model had a z score of -2.05 on GSM8K. Given that I performed 12 actual tests, approximately 0.6 of these should have been significant by chance alone. Moreover, with 12 tests the Bonferroni corrected significance level is 0.004. On average, my 12 tests had a z score of -0.04 with a standard deviation of 1.2 – broadly resembling pure noise. Further, all six permuted tests fell within 0.65 of zero.

What a clean result does and does not indicate

My conclusions are fairly limited. None of the six models learnt the order of these two benchmarks sufficiently for them to be detected by my 40 shard test. Nor did my testing process generate false positives.

Yet I cannot conclude that the models are clean. There are four reasons for this:

  • Blind spot: This test is unable to detect models which have learnt questions in an order other than that of the benchmark. Indeed, this is precisely why the reordered model branch was undertaken.

  • Dose: In my contamination experiment, 24 shards were passed to a model. This occurred eight times and without anything else vying for the model’s attention. Actual pre-training may involve a benchmark or just a few instances of it, alongside trillions of other tokens. Even at this relatively low dose, Oren et al. detected contamination in a 1.4B model. Their tests comprised 1000 test examples [1]. My test was thus almost certainly not as sensitive as theirs as I used 40 shards and 10 permutations.

  • Format: I formatted each example as text stating ‘Question: ... Answer: ...’. Although training data may differ in format from this, I am unsure how resilient order learning is to changes in format.

  • Sample size: Increasing both the number of shards and permutations would improve test sensitivity. However, to allow all models to be tested on a free Colab GPU, I deliberately limited these numbers.

If you wish to test a model in this way, the two functions detailed above encapsulate the technique. All that is required is a benchmark in original order, a method of splitting it into shards and some GPU time — around half an hour per model. Should a model achieve a z score of >3 and there is no obvious reason for it to have encountered test data, further investigation is merited. Yet a near-zero z score is not as informative as it may seem.

summary: 本文提出一种新颖的统计方法，通过衡量模型是否偏好基准测试题目的原始顺序，来检测 LLM 基准污染。该方法将基准测试划分为按顺序排列的「分片」，并生成随机排列，以比较模型赋予题目的对数概率。作者根据原始顺序胜过多少种排列来计算 z 分数，并在 GSM8K 和 ARC-Challenge 数据集上测试了 6 款开源模型：Pythia-1.4B、Qwen2.5-0.5B、Qwen2.5-1.5B、TinyLlama-1.1B、SmolLM2-1.7B 和 Phi-2。作者还使用 Pythia-410M 开展了受控污染实验：在 24 个 GSM8K 分片上训练后，经过 1 个 epoch，z 分数从 -0.8 升至 5.7。然而，如果每个 epoch 都以打乱后的顺序训练相同分片，z 分数便降至 0.1，暴露出该测试的一个盲点。研究得出结论：显著的 z 分数（>3）表明模型可能受到污染，但接近零的分数并不能保证模型没有受到污染，因为该方法的检测灵敏度有限，还会受到格式变化和样本量不足等因素的影响。

mainPoints.point: 基于顺序的污染检测通过 z 分数判断模型是否偏好基准测试题目的原始顺序
mainPoints.explanation: 该测试将基准测试划分为多个分片，并为每个分片生成 10 种随机排列，再比较模型赋予各题目的对数概率，以判断模型是否在统计意义上偏好原始顺序。z 分数根据原始顺序胜过的排列数量计算。

mainPoints.point: 受控污染实验验证了该测试的灵敏度：Pythia-410M 在 GSM8K 分片上训练后，z 分数从 -0.8 升至 5.7

mainPoints.point: 6 款实际开源模型均未表现出显著的顺序偏差，但这并不能证明它们没有受到污染
